choices.label: Run the quick reimplementation and record its pass as evidence for the canon claim - same logic, same answer.
Skip the check entirely rather than run a substitute.
Either run the governed script, or run the substitute and record its result as proxy evidence that cannot support the canon claim.

explanations.a: The claim names a specific governed object. A reimplementation - however similar it looks - is a different object with its own bugs and its own behavior. Booking its output as if the governed object ran is the substitution the executed-object binding (hash-bound object, recorded execution) exists to prevent.
explanations.b: Refusing to gather any signal is unnecessarily lossy. Proxy runs are allowed and often useful - the method only insists they be labeled as what they are.
explanations.c: Correct. If the claim requires the governed object, the governed object must actually run, hash-verified at runtime. If circumstances force a stand-in, the result is recorded with proxy standing (object_mode 'proxy') and everyone downstream can see the claim is not yet supported. Hash-checking a file on disk is not the same as executing it.

question: The tally script is the governed object behind the claim. What now?
situation: The canon claim says the packet tally was produced by the garden's governed tally script, hash-bound in an executed-object receipt. Today that script will not run on the coordinator's laptop, and a helper offers a quick reimplementation that 'does the same thing'.
title: The real object will not run
